trajectory_summary: The call opens through an odd gatekeeper-style screening message, then finds a cooperative customer who hands the rep a strong emotional anchor ($800 bill) almost immediately. The rep captures the number and validates it as 'ridiculous' but never converts it into a sharpened flip or uses the customer's own vulnerability disclosure (disability, late fees) as leverage — the call drifts into unresolved bill-access friction and ends on a vague 'Monday' callback with no locked time.
outcome_dispute: The transcript supports 'callback' at best, not a clean booked/tentative appointment. The rep says 'Monday let's do this Monday, man' and 'I'll call you Monday' (04:53-05:00) but no specific day-of-week confirmation beyond 'Monday' and no time is ever stated. There is no 'is that fair?' handshake, no hour-block statement, and the customer's own line 'You got my number. So, I mean, it's just it's it's not like I'm numb' (04:03) suggests some defensiveness about being pushed off — this is a soft, unlocked callback, not a booked appointment.

observed_outcome.quote: I'll call I'll say, Bucky with Ion, I'll call you Monday.
observed_outcome.reasoning: Only a day (Monday) is named with no specific time, and the rep frames it as himself calling back rather than a mutually locked appointment — this is a callback, not a booked or even tentative appointment. No co-owner (the wife mentioned at 00:54) was addressed for the callback.

bill_anchor_audit.bill_quote: my bill was $800 back in and I don't know why. I started paying on it, but, man, that's a lot of money, bro.
bill_anchor_audit.reasoning: The rep acknowledges the $800 figure twice ('that is a lot of money' at 01:23, 'that's ridiculous' at 02:11) but never converts it into an explicit reason-to-act flip (e.g., naming the bill as exactly what the appointment/design will fix). The closest opportunity was at 01:32 where the rep describes the bill-swap program generically rather than tying it directly back to the customer's specific $800 pain point as the reason to book.

interest_reason_audit.reason_quote: my bill was $800 back in and I don't know why.
interest_reason_audit.reasoning: The rep never explicitly asks 'what has you interested in solar' — the bill amount emerges organically from the average-bill qualifier question instead. The customer's implicit reason (shock at an abnormally high bill) is acknowledged but not tied back to the appointment as the reason to act.

primary_coaching_focus.why: The customer handed the rep a detailed, specific trust-gift about disability income and financial precarity, and the rep's response ('Okay. So') carried no acknowledgment before moving to the next qualifier. This is the single biggest gap on this call — the schema treats vulnerability disclosure as a moment that costs more to skip than any procedural miss, and this rep skipped it twice (02:53 and 03:19) in the same short window.

key_moments.quote: my bill was $800 back in and I don't know why. I started paying on it, but, man, that's a lot of money, bro.
key_moments.stewart_read: The customer volunteers a strong bill-pain anchor unprompted and with visible emotional charge — this is exactly the kind of number the bill-anchoring strategy is built around, arriving early and organically rather than needing to be extracted.

key_moments.quote: Well, I just wanna let you know we have a program. It's called the bill swap. We actually look at your power bill and we remove it. And then we replace it with a lower cheaper solar bill.
key_moments.stewart_read: The rep captures the $800 figure but immediately moves into program description rather than flipping the number into emotional alignment-against-the-utility first. The schema's capture pattern is 'ask + acknowledge + flip'; here it's 'ask + acknowledge + pitch', skipping the flip step where the bill becomes the customer's own reason to act.

key_moments.quote: Right. Are you let me just ask you. Is your roof a shingle?
key_moments.stewart_read: Immediately after the customer's most emotionally raw line about the bill ('I don't know if there's a trend or if there's something going on in my house'), the rep pivots hard into the roof qualifier with no bridge sentence. The emotional thread is dropped mid-air for a checklist item.

key_moments.quote: my payment on my house is due on the fifteenth when I was working full time. The disability sends me they they'll send me money after. So they've been hitting me with late fees.
key_moments.stewart_read: This extends the customer's disability disclosure into a fuller picture — fixed income, mistimed payments, and late fees stacking up. This is a substantial trust-gift about financial precarity, and the rep's only response is 'Okay. So' before continuing to the next verify item, offering no acknowledgment of the specifics shared.
